claim: Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales belong to the classically monoderm Firmicutes but possess outer membranes with lipopolysaccharide (LPS-OM).
source: The Negativicutes and the Halanaerobiales belong to the classically monoderm Firmicutes, but possess outer membranes with lipopolysaccharide (LPS-OM).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 1 and genomic analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales form two phylogenetically distinct lineages, each close to different monoderm relatives.
source: Here, we show that they form two phylogenetically distinct lineages, each close to different monoderm relatives.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phylogenetic analysis in Figure 2 showing distinct branching patterns.

claim: Core LPS biosynthesis enzymes in Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales were inherited vertically, as in the majority of bacterial phyla.
source: In contrast, their core LPS biosynthesis enzymes were inherited vertically, as in the majority of bacterial phyla.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of LPS core genes in Figure 4 showing vertical inheritance patterns.

claim: The LPS-OMs of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales are remnants of an ancient diderm cell envelope that was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that the LPS-OMs of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales are remnants of an ancient diderm cell envelope that was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes, and that the monoderm phenotype in this phylum is a derived character that arose multiple times independently through OM loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analyses and the pattern of LPS gene inheritance.

claim: The monoderm phenotype in Firmicutes is a derived character that arose multiple times independently through OM loss.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that the LPS-OMs of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales are remnants of an ancient diderm cell envelope that was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes, and that the monoderm phenotype in this phylum is a derived character that arose multiple times independently through OM loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic placement of diderm lineages among monoderm relatives, requiring multiple independent losses.

claim: Megamonas rupellensis displays a diderm-type cell envelope architecture with cytoplasmic membrane, periplasm with thin peptidoglycan layer, and outer membrane.
source: In a cross section from inside to outside, the densely packed cytoplasm of M. rupellensis is surrounded by a cytoplasmic membrane followed by the periplasm with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an OM (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Halanaerobium saccharolyticum displays a diderm cell envelope with densely packed cytoplasm enclosed by a membrane surrounded by a relatively electron lucent periplasm with visible peptidoglycan.
source: Thin sections of H. saccharolyticum also revealed a diderm cell envelope with a densely packed cytoplasm enclosed by a membrane surrounded by a relatively electron lucent periplasm so that the thin line representing the peptidoglycan is clearly visible (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pilus-like structures were detected in Megamonas rupellensis.
source: Furthermore, pilus-like structures could be detected, as well as another electron dense layer outside the OM, which might correspond either to the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or an S-layer.
evidence: This is observed in electron microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: The Negativicutes branched within Class Clostridia, specifically related to Peptococcaceae and other incertae-sedis clostridial families.
source: In fact, the Negativicutes branched within Class Clostridia, specifically related to Peptococcaceae and other incertae-sedis clostridial families (PP = 1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown by the Bayesian phylogenetic tree in Figure 2 with high posterior probability support.

claim: Members of Peptococcaceae have monoderm phenotype and no homologues of OM markers.
source: As opposed to the diderm nature of Negativicutes, the members of Peptococcaceae have monoderm phenotype (Vos et al., 2009) and no homologues of OM markers.
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and genomic analysis.

claim: The Halanaerobiales emerged as a distinct, well-supported, and deep-branching lineage of the Firmicutes.
source: In contrast, the Halanaerobiales emerged as a distinct, well-supported, and deep-branching lineage of the Firmicutes (PP = 0.99, Figure 2), robustly grouped with the order Natranaerobiales (PP = 1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown by the Bayesian phylogenetic tree in Figure 2 with high posterior probability support.

claim: Halanaerobiales are robustly grouped with the order Natranaerobiales.
source: In contrast, the Halanaerobiales emerged as a distinct, well-supported, and deep-branching lineage of the Firmicutes (PP = 0.99, Figure 2), robustly grouped with the order Natranaerobiales (PP = 1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown by the Bayesian phylogenetic tree in Figure 2 with posterior probability of 1.

claim: Natranaerobiales are moderately halophilic Firmicutes that appear monoderm under the microscope and have no homologues of OM markers.
source: Natranaerobiales are a poorly known group of moderately halophilic Firmicutes that appear monoderm under the microscope (Mesbah et al., 2007) and have no homologues of OM markers.
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and genomic analysis.

claim: Two alternative topologies presenting a clustering of Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes were strongly rejected by the data.
source: Importantly, the two alternative topologies presenting a clustering of Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes (H6 and N6) were strongly rejected by the data, as well as all topologies where the Halanaerobiales were moved away from the root of the Firmicutes tree (H2-H5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Additional Data), consistent with the separate origins of the two diderm lineages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AU topology tests shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A large genomic locus is conserved between Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes that is not present in monoderm Firmicutes.
source: Interestingly, synteny analyses revealed a large genomic locus that is conserved between Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes, and is not present in monoderm Firmicutes (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown by synteny analysis in Figure 3.

claim: The genes coding for the first four steps of LPS synthesis (lpxABCD) display a conserved synteny in diderm Bacteria at very large evolutionary distances.
source: However, the genes coding for the first four steps of LPS synthesis (lpxABCD) display a conserved synteny in diderm Bacteria at very large evolutionary distances, suggesting that they have similar evolutionary histories (Opiyo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and confirmed by synteny analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Homologues of the four core LPS coding genes are present in 26 major bacterial phyla.
source: As compared to what could be previously inferred from available genomic data (Sutcliffe, 2010; Opiyo et al., 2010), we show the presence of homologues of the four core LPS coding genes in 26 major bacterial phyla, eight of which evidenced for the first time: Thermodesulfobacteria, Fibrobacteres, Ignavibacteria, Nitrospina, Chrysiogenetes, Cloacimonetes, Atribacteria, and Armatimonadetes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by homology searches across 121 representative bacterial genomes.

claim: Eight bacterial phyla show evidence of LPS genes for the first time: Thermodesulfobacteria, Fibrobacteres, Ignavibacteria, Nitrospina, Chrysiogenetes, Cloacimonetes, Atribacteria, and Armatimonadetes.
source: As compared to what could be previously inferred from available genomic data (Sutcliffe, 2010; Opiyo et al., 2010), we show the presence of homologues of the four core LPS coding genes in 26 major bacterial phyla, eight of which evidenced for the first time: Thermodesulfobacteria, Fibrobacteres, Ignavibacteria, Nitrospina, Chrysiogenetes, Cloacimonetes, Atribacteria, and Armatimonadetes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by homology searches in this study.

claim: Only four major bacterial phyla appear to lack the coding capacity for LPS: Thermotogae, Caldiserica, Chloroflexi/Thermomicrobia, and Actinobacteria.
source: This suggests that LPS-diderm cell envelopes might be even more widespread in Bacteria than currently thought, leaving only four major phyla that appear to lack the coding capacity for LPS: Thermotogae, Caldiserica, Chloroflexi/Thermomicrobia, and Actinobacteria (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on absence of LPS genes in genomic searches.

claim: The Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes form a well-supported monophyletic cluster in the LPS gene tree.
source: Consistently, the Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes also form a well-supported monophyletic cluster (PP = 1, Figure 4), with internal branching pattern matching their respective reference species phylogeny shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This is shown by the Bayesian phylogenetic tree of LPS core genes in Figure 4.

claim: Present-day monoderm Firmicutes emerged from diderm ancestors via not less than five independent losses of the OM.
source: The inclusion of a second diderm lineage in our analysis allows us to strengthen and extend this scenario, and to infer that present-day monoderm Firmicutes would have emerged from diderm ancestors via not less than five independent losses of the OM (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology and the distribution of diderm/monoderm phenotypes.

claim: Both Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales have a complete set of genes for the synthesis of the Lipid A moiety and inner core of LPS.
source: Both Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales have a complete set of genes for the synthesis of the Lipid A moiety and inner core of LPS (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis and shown schematically in Figure 5.

claim: The lack of lpxH and the presence of lpxI suggests that Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales use an alternative route for lipid A-core synthesis.
source: The lack of lpxH and the presence of lpxI suggests that they use a recently-described alternative route for lipid A-core synthesis found in members of various bacterial lineages (Metzger and Raetz, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence/absence of specific genes and supported by literature citation.

claim: The lpx gene cluster in diderm Firmicutes includes a fabZ homologue, which encodes an enzyme involved in a key step of fatty acid synthesis.
source: Moreover, the lpx gene cluster also includes a fabZ homologue, which encodes an enzyme involved in a key step of fatty acid synthesis and is also present in monoderm Firmicutes (Parsons and Rock, 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis and supported by literature citation.

claim: All Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales have a conserved Lpt four-gene cluster next to the LPS synthesis genes.
source: In all Negativicutes and Hanaerobiales, we identified a conserved Lpt four-gene cluster next to the LPS synthesis genes (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: No clear homologues of the OM components LptD/E were found in the gene cluster or elsewhere in the genomes of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales.
source: However, we could not find any clear homologues of the OM components LptD/E in the gene cluster or elsewhere in the genomes.
evidence: This is based on homology searches in genomic data.

claim: All analyzed Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales genomes possess a single BamA homologue, which is part of a gene cluster with a homologue of TamB, and up to three homologues of the Skp chaperone.
source: We found that all analyzed Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales genomes possess a single BamA homologue, which is part of a gene cluster with a homologue of TamB, and up to three homologues of the Skp chaperone (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The same gene arrangement (TamB/BamA/Skp) has been observed in Spirochaetes and many other bacterial phyla.
source: Interestingly, the same gene arrangement (TamB/BamA/Skp) has been observed in Spirochaetes (Selkrig et al., 2012), as well as in many other bacterial phyla (Heinz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: Halanaerobiales contain in the conserved genomic locus up to three proteins with an SLH domain that likely represent distant homologues of Negativicutes OmpM.
source: We found that Halanaerobiales also contain in the conserved genomic locus up to three proteins with an SLH domain (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1). These likely represent distant homologues of Negativicutes OmpM and are priority targets for experimental validation to confirm the presence of an OmpM-dependent system for OM anchoring in this deep-emerging lineage of the Firmicutes.
evidence: This is inferred from domain analysis and genomic synteny shown in Figure 3.

claim: OmpM-like proteins might represent a widespread and ancient PG-OM anchoring system, possibly ancestral to the Braun's lipoprotein-based system.
source: OmpM-like proteins might therefore represent a widespread and ancient PG-OM anchoring system (Figure 5), possibly ancestral to the Braun's lipoprotein-based system.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of similar proteins in distantly related phyla.

claim: Most Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales strains analyzed in this study are flagellated and have a complete set of genes coding for the flagellum machinery.
source: Most Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales strains analyzed in this study are flagellated (Vos et al., 2009) and have in fact a complete set of genes coding for the flagellum machinery, most of which embedded in an operon arrangement that is distinctive of B. subtilis and other monoderm Firmicutes, in particular the presence of the two rod assembly genes flgB and flgC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Mukherjee and Kearns, 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales possess homologues of the three genes coding for the P and L rings typical of diderm flagella (flgH, flgI, and flgA), organized in a second conserved six-genes cluster.
source: However, Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales also possess homologues of the three genes coding for the P and L rings typical of diderm flagella, flgH, flgI, and flgA, organized in a second conserved six-genes cluster that also contains the rod components flgF, flgG, and flgJ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales might possess flagella with chimeric monoderm/diderm features.
source: These data suggest that Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales might possess flagella with chimeric monoderm/diderm features (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both monoderm-type and diderm-type flagellar genes.

claim: Both Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales have a conserved genomic locus that presumably codes for all essential components of a type IV pilus.
source: Both Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales have a conserved genomic locus that presumably codes for all essential components of a type IV pilus (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), consistently with the visualization of a potential pilus structure by microscopy in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and microscopy in Figure 1.

claim: All Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales possess a homologue of PilQ, the secretin, which is present in the type IV pilus gene cluster.
source: The gene cluster is similar to those present in their closely related monoderm relatives, to the exception of the inclusion of a homologue of PilQ, the secretin, which is present in all Negativicutes and Hanalerobiales (Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: No homologues of LolA nor of LolB were found in any of the Negativicutes genomes.
source: We found no homologues of LolA nor of LolB in any of the Negativicutes genomes, confirming previous reports (Campbell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on homology searches in genomic data and confirmed by literature citation.

claim: Homologues of LolA were found in each of the analyzed Halanaerobiales genomes, which correlate to the presence of Lnt homologues.
source: In contrast, we found homologues of LolA in each of the analyzed Halanaerobiales genomes, which correlate to the presence of Lnt homologues (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by homology searches in genomic data.

claim: A conserved gene cluster likely coding for a complete Lol system was identified in most Halanaerobiales genomes.
source: By looking at the genomic surroundings of these LolA homologues, we identified a conserved gene cluster in most Halanaerobiales genomes, which likely code for a complete Lol system, notably the two ABC transporter permeases (LolC/E) and one ATPase (LolD) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic synteny analysis.

claim: Halanaerobiales may harbor a functional Lol system.
source: These analyses suggest that Halanaerobiales may harbor a functional Lol system (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of key Lol system components in genomic data.

claim: Three genes encoding proteins with unclear annotation display a conserved synteny within the large conserved genomic cluster and are present in all Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales genomes while absent from monoderm Firmicutes.
source: Finally, three genes encoding proteins with unclear annotation display a conserved synteny within the large conserved genomic cluster (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1) and are present in all Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales genomes (Supplementary file 1), while absent from monoderm Firmicutes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis in Figure 3 and genomic surveys.

claim: In Selenomonas ruminantium the abundant OmpM protein appears to replace the important function of Braun's lipoprotein in anchoring the OM to the cell peptidoglycan through a link with cadaverine.
source: In Selenomonas ruminantium the abundant OmpM protein appears to replace the important function of Braun's lipoprotein in anchoring the OM to the cell peptidoglycan through a link with cadaverine (Kojima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Veillonella is one of the most abundant components of the human oral flora.
source: Veillonella is one of the most abundant components of the human oral flora (Tanner et al., 2011), and a common inhabitant of the intestinal microbiome (van den Bogert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: Veillonella is a common inhabitant of the intestinal microbiome.
source: Veillonella is one of the most abundant components of the human oral flora (Tanner et al., 2011), and a common inhabitant of the intestinal microbiome (van den Bogert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Veillonella has been recently associated with maturation of the immune system and partial protection of asthma in infants.
source: Together with other gut microbes, it has been recently associated with maturation of the immune system and partial protection of asthma in infants (Arrieta et al., 2015), but can also develop into an opportunistic pathogen (Hirai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Veillonella can develop into an opportunistic pathogen.
source: Together with other gut microbes, it has been recently associated with maturation of the immune system and partial protection of asthma in infants (Arrieta et al., 2015), but can also develop into an opportunistic pathogen (Hirai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Several Negativicutes members such as Dialister, Selenomonas, Mitsuokella, and Anaeroglobus show increased incidence in oral tract disease linked to biofilm formation.
source: Several other Negativicutes members such as Dialister, Selenomonas, Mitsuokella, and Anaeroglobus show increased incidence in oral tract disease linked to biofilm formation (Griffen et al., 2012) and involvement in other infections (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: The Halanaerobiales are a poorly studied group of moderate halophilic, strictly anaerobic Firmicutes that were isolated from saline environments such as lake and lagoon sediments, and oil reservoirs.
source: Interestingly, the Negativicutes are not the only diderm lineage in the Firmicutes. The Halanaerobiales are a poorly studied group of moderate halophilic, strictly anaerobic Firmicutes that were isolated from saline environments such as lake and lagoon sediments, and oil reservoirs (Oren, 2006; Roush et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: Halanaerobiales display a diderm-type cell envelope, with a thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane.
source: Similarly to the Negativicutes, they display a diderm-type cell envelope, with a thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane (Cayol et al., 1994; Zeikus et al., 1983; Zhilina et al., 1992, Zhilina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: The very first observation and use of the term 'outer membrane' has been based on studies of Veillonella.
source: Curiously, the very first observation and use of the term 'outer membrane' has been based on studies of Veillonella (Bladen and Mergenhagen, 1964).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: An outer membrane forms only transiently during sporulation in classically monoderm Firmicutes such as Bacillus subtilis.
source: They showed that, while an outer membrane forms only transiently during sporulation in classically monoderm Firmicutes such as Bacillus subtilis, it is retained in A. longum leading to its diderm phenotype (Tocheva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The outer membrane is retained in Acetonema longum during sporulation leading to its diderm phenotype.
source: They showed that, while an outer membrane forms only transiently during sporulation in classically monoderm Firmicutes such as Bacillus subtilis, it is retained in A. longum leading to its diderm phenotype (Tocheva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: As much as 7% of the BLAST top hits in the genome of Acidaminococcus intestini were from Proteobacteria, the majority of which corresponded to functions related to OM biogenesis.
source: In contrast, a recent analysis of the genome of the Negativicute Acidaminococcus intestini revealed that as much as 7% of the BLAST top hits were from Proteobacteria, the majority of which corresponded to functions related to OM biogenesis, concluding to a possible acquisition of the OM in Negativicutes by horizontal gene transfer (Campbell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The bacterial envelope is involved in key housekeeping functions such as physical integrity, cell division, motility, substrate uptake and secretion, and cell-cell communication.
source: The bacterial envelope is one of the oldest and most essential cellular components, involved in key housekeeping functions such as physical integrity, cell division, motility, substrate uptake and secretion, and cell-cell communication (Silhavy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Bacteria show substantial differences in their cell envelope architectures, among which the most dramatic one is the presence of one (monoderm) or two (diderm) membranes.
source: Yet, bacteria show substantial differences in their cell envelope architectures, among which the most dramatic one is the presence of one (monoderm) or two (diderm) membranes (Sutcliffe, 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, teichoic and lipoteichoic acids are embedded in a thick peptidoglycan wall.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, teichoic and lipoteichoic acids are embedded in a thick peptidoglycan wall, while in Escherichia coli a thin peptidoglycan layer is surrounded by an outer membrane (OM) whose biogenesis and functioning involve a complex system of synthesis and transport for LPS, lipoproteins, and OM proteins (OMPs) (Silhavy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: In Escherichia coli a thin peptidoglycan layer is surrounded by an outer membrane whose biogenesis and functioning involve a complex system of synthesis and transport for LPS, lipoproteins, and OM proteins.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, teichoic and lipoteichoic acids are embedded in a thick peptidoglycan wall, while in Escherichia coli a thin peptidoglycan layer is surrounded by an outer membrane (OM) whose biogenesis and functioning involve a complex system of synthesis and transport for LPS, lipoproteins, and OM proteins (OMPs) (Silhavy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The majority of bacterial phyla seem to possess two membranes.
source: The fact that the majority of phyla seem to possess two membranes might favor the diderm-first scenario, although the actual diversity of cell envelopes in Bacteria remains largely unexplored (Sutcliffe, 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The lack of a robustly resolved phylogeny for Bacteria has left the relationships between diderm and monoderm phyla unclear.
source: However, the lack of a robustly resolved phylogeny for Bacteria, notably the uncertainty on its root and the nature of the earliest branches, has left the relationships between diderm and monoderm phyla unclear, and not allowed to define in which direction and how many times this transition occurred.
evidence: This represents a known limitation in the field.

claim: The Negativicutes have been identified in various anaerobic environments, such as soil and lake sediments, industrial waste, and animal digestive tract.
source: The Negativicutes have been identified in various anaerobic environments, such as soil and lake sediments, industrial waste, and animal digestive tract (Vos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Veillonella was first described in 1898 by Veillon and Zuber.
source: Their best-characterized member is Veillonella, first described in 1898 by Veillon and Zuber (Veillon and Zuber, 1898).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The core LPS genes were present in the ancestor of each diderm phylum and inter-phylum horizontal gene transfers were surprisingly rare during bacterial evolution.
source: However, it is largely in agreement with bacterial systematics, showing the monophyly of major phyla (Figure 4). This pattern indicates that the core LPS genes were present in the ancestor of each of these diderm phyla, and that inter-phylum horizontal gene transfers were surprisingly rare during bacterial evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic pattern of LPS genes matching organismal phylogeny.

claim: The diderm cell envelopes of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales show an intriguing combination of diderm and monoderm features.
source: In this respect, the presence of the conserved OM locus helped annotation greatly and provided important insights into the unique nature of the cell envelopes of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales, which show both specific characteristics as well as an intriguing combination of diderm and monoderm features (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genomic analysis of various OM-related systems.

claim: The conserved genomic proximity of fabZ with lpxC is a strong indication that these two proteins interact in diderm Firmicutes, likely in a common process that regulates the phospholipid/LPS balance of the OM.
source: Because FabZ acts on a substrate that is shared with the lipid A pathway, its conserved genomic proximity with LpxC is a strong indication that these two proteins interact in diderm Firmicutes, likely in a common process that regulates the phospholipid/LPS balance of the OM as described in E. coli (Klein et al., 2014; Ogura et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from genomic synteny and comparison with E. coli, supported by literature citations.

claim: The genomic location of MsbA homologues suggests that they are likely bona fide MsbA functional equivalents in diderm Firmicutes.
source: Although these are part of the very large protein family of ABC transporters that is also present in monoderm Firmicutes, their genomic location suggests that they are likely bona fide MsbA functional equivalents in diderm Firmicutes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from genomic synteny within the LPS gene cluster.

claim: Either LptD/E homologues in diderm Firmicutes are too distantly related to be identified by sequence similarity, or Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales employ a non-homologous system to address LPS to the OM.
source: Either these are too distantly related to being identified by sequence similarity, or Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales employ a non-homologous system to address LPS to the OM.
evidence: This is speculated based on the absence of identifiable homologues.

claim: It is difficult to assess functional homology and infer with confidence if diderm Firmicutes are able to make smooth LPS.
source: Moreover, although we could identify some homologues in the genomes of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales, these are part of very large protein families and are shared with other pathways, making it difficult to assess functional homology and infer with confidence if diderm Firmicutes are able to make smooth LPS.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation based on the analysis of O-antigen pathway genes.

claim: No homologues of the associated lipoproteins of the Bam complex (BamBCDE) were found in the gene cluster nor elsewhere in the genomes of diderm Firmicutes.
source: However, we could not find any homologues of the associated lipoproteins of the Bam complex (BamBCDE) in the gene cluster nor elsewhere in the genomes of diderm Firmicutes, though it is known that these are not well conserved outside Proteobacteria (Webb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on homology searches and supported by literature citation.

claim: TamA has one POTRA domain only and was shown to be anchored to the OM and to form a two-pathway system together with the IM protein TamB to promote T5SS autotransporter assembly and secretion.
source: In Proteobacteria, a close paralogue of BamA was recently discovered, called TamA, which has one POTRA domain only, and was shown to be anchored to the OM and to form a two-pathway system together with the IM protein TamB to promote T5SS autotransporter assembly and secretion (Selkrig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: TamB was present very early in bacterial evolution and functioned with BamA, while TamA would have arisen more recently in Proteobacteria through gene duplication.
source: Based on the large taxonomic distribution of TamB homologues, it has been recently proposed that this protein was present very early in bacterial evolution, and functioned with BamA, while TamA would have arisen more recently in Proteobacteria through gene duplication (Heinz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The inference of a potential TamB/BamA/Skp system in the ancestor of the Firmicutes strengthens the hypothesis of an ancestral bi-functional role for BamA in both autotransporter secretion and OMP assembly.
source: The inference of a potential TamB/BamA/Skp system in the ancestor of the Firmicutes strengthens the hypothesis of an ancestral bi-functional role for BamA in both autotransporter secretion (together with TamB) and OMP assembly (together with Skp) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the conserved gene arrangement in diderm Firmicutes and other phyla.

claim: In Selenomonas ruminantium OmpM results from the fusion of a C-terminal porin domain and an N-terminal S-layer homologous (SLH) domain with an unusual inward orientation towards the periplasm.
source: In S. ruminantium OmpM results from the fusion of a C-terminal porin domain and an N-terminal S-layer homologous (SLH) domain with an unusual inward orientation towards the periplasm where it drives the correct anchoring of the OM to the peptidoglycan layer via specific interactions with the peptidoglycan-covalently-bound cadaverine (Kalmokoff et al., 2009; Kojima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: There have been early reports of distantly related proteins with a domain arrangement similar to that of diderm Firmicutes OmpM and a proposed similar function in Cyanobacteria and in Thermotogae.
source: Interestingly, there have been early reports of distantly related proteins with a domain arrangement similar to that of diderm Firmicutes OmpM and a proposed similar function in Cyanobacteria (Hansel et al., 1998) and in Thermotogae (Engel et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: The monoderm-type flagellum has been mostly studied in B. subtilis.
source: The monoderm-type flagellum has been mostly studied in B. subtilis (Mukherjee and Kearns, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The monoderm flagellum is very similar in overall structure and number of components to the flagellum of diderm bacteria, with the exception of the absence of the rings P and L.
source: It is very similar in overall structure and number of components to the flagellum of diderm bacteria, to the exception of the absence of the rings P and L, the first spanning the periplasm and the second spanning the OM, which are coded by flgH, flgI, and flgA and are totally absent in monoderm flagella.
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: It is unknown how flagellar insertion in the PG layer takes place in B. subtilis.
source: Another difference is the absence of the rod cap and flagellar-specific peptidoglycan hydrolases, which allow insertion in the PG layer in diderm bacteria, and it is unknown how this process takes place in the thick PG layer of B. subtilis (Mukherjee and Kearns, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The flagella of diderm Firmicutes are closely related to those of their monoderm relatives.
source: This indicates that the flagella of diderm Firmicutes are closely related to those of their monoderm relatives.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared operon arrangement with monoderm Firmicutes.

claim: Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales flagella may represent ancestral motility structures that adapted to loss of the OM in present-day monoderm Firmicutes lineages.
source: They may represent ancestral motility structures that adapted to loss of the OM in present-day monoderm Firmicutes lineages, possibly through a single excision of the flgH, flgI, and flgA gene cluster from the conserved genomic locus.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of both monoderm and diderm flagellar features.

claim: Representatives of the monoderm Firmicutes lineages most closely related to Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes still retain an flgJ homologue that may represent a remnant of the ancestral diderm system for rod insertion.
source: Consistently with this hypothesis, we observed that representatives of the monoderm Firmicutes lineages that are most closely related to Halanaerobiales (i.e. Natranaerobiales: N. thermophilus) and Negativicutes (i.e. Peptococcaceae: Therminicola potens) still retain an flgJ homologue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) that may represent a remnant of the ancestral diderm system for rod insertion, which would have been lost in B. subtilis and other monoderm flagellated Firmicutes.
evidence: This is inferred from genomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Type IV pili have very similar components in diderm and monoderm bacteria, with the exception of PilQ (secretin), which in diderm bacteria forms a channel that spans the OM.
source: A similar, although less clear-cut, scenario could be inferred for type IV pili. These have very similar components in diderm and monoderm bacteria, to the exception of PilQ (also called secretin), which in diderm bacteria forms a channel that spans the OM and through which the pilus is assembled (Melville and Craig, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: In Firmicutes, it is unclear how the pilus passes through the thick peptidoglycan layer, and if a channel-forming protein is present.
source: In Firmicutes, it is unclear how the pilus passes through the thick peptidoglycan layer, and if a channel-forming protein is present (Melville and Craig, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: The type IV pili of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales may pass through the OM by a secretin-based mechanism similar to that of classical diderm bacteria.
source: These data suggest that the type IV pili of Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales may pass through the OM by a secretin-based mechanism similar to that of classical diderm bacteria (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of PilQ homologues in the pilus gene cluster.

claim: Lipoproteins are a major class of membrane proteins that play important physiological roles and are widespread in bacteria.
source: Lipoproteins are a major class of membrane proteins that play important physiological roles and are widespread in bacteria (Buddelmeijer, 2015; Okuda and Tokuda, 2011; Sutcliffe et al., 2012; Zückert, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Tri-acylated lipoproteins are preferentially targeted to the OM in diderm bacteria via the Lol machinery.
source: Tri-acylated lipoproteins are preferentially targeted to the OM in diderm bacteria via the Lol machinery.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about lipoprotein trafficking.

claim: The presence of LolA homologues is indicative of a functional Lol system.
source: While LolCDE are part of the large protein family of ABC transporters, the presence of LolA homologues is indicative of a functional Lol system (Sutcliffe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: It is possible that Negativicutes do not address lipoproteins to the OM or that they use a still unknown, non-homologous system.
source: It is possible that Negativicutes do not address lipoproteins to the OM or that they use a still unknown, non-homologous system.
evidence: This is speculated based on the absence of Lol system components.

claim: No homologues of LolB were found in the genomic locus or elsewhere in the Halanaerobiales genomes, although this protein is not well conserved in bacteria.
source: We could not find any homologues of LolB in the genomic locus or elsewhere in the Halanaerobiales genomes, although this protein is not well conserved in bacteria (Sutcliffe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on homology searches and supported by literature citation.

claim: Three conserved proteins in the genomic cluster might be involved in OM biogenesis and functioning in diderm Firmicutes and are priority targets for experimental characterization.
source: These proteins might be involved in OM biogenesis and functioning in diderm Firmicutes and are priority targets for experimental characterization.
evidence: This is speculated based on their conserved presence in diderm Firmicutes and absence in monoderm relatives.

claim: One of the conserved proteins belongs to COG0816, annotated as 'Predicted endonuclease involved in recombination'.
source: The first one belongs to COG0816, which is annotated as 'Predicted endonuclease involved in recombination (possible Holliday junction resolvase in Mycoplasmas and B. subtilis)'.
evidence: This is based on COG annotation.

claim: One of the conserved proteins belongs to COG4372, annotated as 'Uncharacterized conserved protein, contains DUF3084 domain'.
source: The second one belongs to COG4372, which is annotated as 'Uncharacterized conserved protein, contains DUF3084 domain'.
evidence: This is based on COG annotation.

claim: One of the conserved proteins belongs to COG750, annotated as 'Predicted membrane-associated Zn-dependent proteases 1', and is predicted to be in the OM.
source: The third one belongs to COG750, which is annotated as "Predicted membrane-associated Zn-dependent proteases 1", and is predicted to be in the OM by the PSORT prediction software (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on COG annotation and computational prediction.

claim: The complexity of the diderm cell envelope with respect to a perceived more 'rudimentary' monoderm type, together with its higher resistance toward antibiotics, are arguments usually put forward to propose that the OM is a relatively late invention in Bacteria.
source: The complexity of the diderm cell envelope with respect to a perceived more 'rudimentary' monoderm type, together with its higher resistance toward antibiotics, are arguments usually put forward to propose that the OM is a relatively late invention in Bacteria (Koch, 2003; Gupta, 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: Diderm phyla outnumber monoderm ones and span a large fraction of bacterial diversity, including early emerging lineages.
source: However, it is now evident that diderm phyla outnumber monoderm ones, and span a large fraction of bacterial diversity, including early emerging lineages (Sutcliffe, 2010; Errington, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citations.

claim: The deep branching of Halanaerobiales and the still limited genomic coverage for this group makes them a priority target for further exploration as their cell envelopes may retain ancestral characters.
source: The deep branching of Halanaerobiales and the still limited genomic coverage for this group makes them a priority target for further exploration as their cell envelopes may retain ancestral characters.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic position and limited current knowledge.

claim: The availability of genomic data from an ever-wider sampling of bacterial diversity is sensibly changing perspective on the evolution of bacterial cell envelopes.
source: Clearly, the availability of genomic data from an ever-wider sampling of bacterial diversity is sensibly changing perspective on the evolution of bacterial cell envelopes.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation based on the findings of this study.

claim: By revealing the presence of an LPS-OM in the ancestor of Deinococcus/Thermus, this study shows that this phylum does not represent a monoderm-to-diderm intermediate.
source: For example, by revealing the presence of an LPS-OM in the ancestor of Deinococcus/Thermus we show that this phylum does not represent a monoderm-to-diderm intermediate (Gupta, 2011), but rather that LPS was lost in some of their members, a process similar to what likely occurred in Thermotogae (Cavalier-Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of LPS genes in Deinococcus/Thermus.

claim: LPS was lost in some members of Deinococcus/Thermus, a process similar to what likely occurred in Thermotogae.
source: For example, by revealing the presence of an LPS-OM in the ancestor of Deinococcus/Thermus we show that this phylum does not represent a monoderm-to-diderm intermediate (Gupta, 2011), but rather that LPS was lost in some of their members, a process similar to what likely occurred in Thermotogae (Cavalier-Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of LPS genes and supported by literature citation.

claim: Although having an OM is surely advantageous in certain conditions, the diderm cell envelope is a flexible structure that can be modified/simplified during evolution.
source: This indicates that, although having an OM is surely advantageous in certain conditions, the diderm cell envelope is a flexible structure that can be modified/simplified during evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple independent losses of the OM observed in this study.

claim: The gene transfer hypothesis for OM acquisition in diderm Firmicutes would imply a complex scenario consisting of two independent transfers of a very large genomic region.
source: Given the distinct branching of the two diderm lineages in the Firmicutes phylogeny, and the pattern of LPS inheritance similar to all other diderm bacterial phyla, the gene transfer hypothesis would imply a complex scenario consisting of two independent transfers of a very large genomic region, a first one to the ancestor of Halanaerobiales or to the ancestor of Negativicutes, and a second one between these two ancestors, which would have had to coexist at the same time and in the same environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic data and represents an argument against horizontal gene transfer.

claim: The sudden acquisition of an OM has been discussed as mechanistically complicated.
source: The sudden acquisition of an OM has been already discussed as mechanistically complicated (Cavalier-Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: Acquisition of an OM would have required the dramatic modification of an originally monoderm cell envelope through the concerted acquisition of several complex systems at once.
source: This would have in fact required the dramatic modification of an originally monoderm cell envelope through the concerted acquisition of several complex systems at once, not to mention the replacement of the native inner membrane components of these systems or their coordination with the newly acquired ones.
evidence: This is stated as an argument against horizontal gene transfer of the OM.

claim: Not all OM systems involved in OM biogenesis and function in Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales are part of the gene cluster.
source: Moreover, not all OM systems involved in OM biogenesis and function in Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales are part of the gene cluster, and their detailed annotation suggests that their cell envelopes share characteristics with deep-emerging bacterial phyla (e.g. the OmpM porin instead of Braun's lipoprotein for OM tethering), and present a peculiar combination of monoderm/diderm features (e.g. flagella, pili).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genomic analysis of various OM systems.

claim: The OM gene cluster may represent an ancestral genomic locus for OM–related functions.
source: The OM gene cluster may therefore represent an ancestral genomic locus for OM–related functions, and it becomes essential to obtain further experimental characterization of the OM of Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes, as well as many other poorly explored deep emerging bacterial phyla.
evidence: This is inferred from the conserved synteny and the characteristics of the encoded systems.

claim: There are additional OM components that are lineage-specific in Negativicutes and Halanaerobiales and may have been acquired from diderm bacteria thriving in the same environment.
source: Nevertheless, we have analyzed here only a few OM systems shared between Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes in order to infer the nature of the ancestral diderm cell envelope in the Firmicutes. There are surely additional components that are lineage-specific and may have been acquired from diderm bacteria thriving in the same environment.
evidence: This is speculated as a possibility for future investigation.

claim: A spontaneous mutation leading to hypertrophy of the peptidoglycan layer would be sufficient to transform a diderm into a monoderm, through disruption of the attachment of the OM, leading to its loss.
source: It has been proposed that a spontaneous mutation leading to hypertrophy of the peptidoglycan layer would be sufficient to transform a diderm into a monoderm, through disruption of the attachment of the OM, leading to its loss (Cavalier-Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation as a proposed mechanism for OM loss.

claim: Mutations may have affected the ancestral OmpM, causing a de-regulation of OM-PG attachment, facilitating the transition to monoderm.
source: Alternatively, we speculate that mutations may have affected the ancestral OmpM, causing a de-regulation of OM-PG attachment.
evidence: This is speculated as an alternative mechanism for OM loss.

claim: The OM might have been lost in the Firmicutes to increase sporulation and germination efficiency.
source: Tocheva et al. (2011) proposed indeed that the OM might have been lost in the Firmicutes to increase sporulation and germination efficiency (Tocheva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on literature citation.

claim: A link between OM loss and sporulation may explain why there is no current evidence of monoderm lineages within other diderm phyla that do not sporulate.
source: A link between OM loss and sporulation may explain why there is no current evidence of monoderm lineages within other diderm phyla that do not sporulate.
evidence: This is inferred from the association between sporulation and OM loss in Firmicutes.

claim: The cell envelopes of diderm Firmicutes might be the remnants of an ancient type of cellular structure.
source: Our results suggest that the cell envelopes of diderm Firmicutes might be the remnants of an ancient type of cellular structure, adding up to the ones found in the major diderm bacterial phyla.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and genomic analyses.

claim: Diderm Firmicutes seem to have ancestral and simpler cell envelope systems with respect to the well-studied Proteobacteria.
source: Moreover, they seem to have ancestral and simpler cell envelope systems with respect to the well-studied Proteobacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative genomic analysis of OM systems.

claim: Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes are promising new experimental models that will provide precious insights into the processes that have shaped the diversity of diderm and monoderm cell envelopes.
source: Halanaerobiales and Negativicutes are therefore promising new experimental models that will provide precious insights into the processes that have shaped the diversity not only of diderm cell envelopes, but also of monoderm ones.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the findings of the study.
